title: III. Peasant Women Who Have Faith
paragraphs: Down by the wooden portico, which was built onto the outer wall of the precinct, a crowd of about twenty peasant women had gathered. They had heard that the elder was finally coming out, and they stood waiting for him. Two ladies, Madame Hohlakov and her daughter, had come out into the portico as well. They waited in a separate section, set aside for women of rank.

Madame Hohlakov was a rich lady, still young and attractive, and always dressed with taste. She was a little pale, with lively black eyes. She was no more than thirty-three and had been a widow for five years. Her daughter, who was fourteen, was partly paralyzed. The poor girl had not been able to walk for six months, and people wheeled her around in a long reclining chair. She had a charming little face, thin from illness but full of gaiety. Her big dark eyes, with their long lashes, had a mischievous gleam. Her mother had meant to take her abroad since spring, but business over their estate had held them up all summer. They had now been in our town for a week. They had come more on business than out of devotion, but they had already visited Father Zossima once, three days earlier. They knew the elder hardly received anyone. Even so, they had suddenly turned up again and were pleading urgently for “the happiness of looking once again on the great healer.”

The mother sat on a chair next to her daughter’s invalid carriage. Two paces from her stood an old monk. He was not from our monastery but a visitor from some obscure religious house in the far north, and he too had come for the elder’s blessing.

Father Zossima came into the portico and went first straight to the peasants, who were crowded at the bottom of the three steps up to it. He stood on the top step, put on his stole, and began blessing the women as they pressed around him. A crazy woman was brought up to him. The moment she saw the elder, she began to shriek and writhe as if in the pains of childbirth. He laid the stole on her forehead and said a short prayer over her, and at once she grew calm and quiet.

I do not know how it is now, but in my childhood I often saw and heard these “possessed” women in villages and monasteries. They were brought to mass, and there they would squeal and bark like dogs so loudly that the whole church heard them. But when the sacrament was carried in and they were led up to it, the “possession” stopped at once, and for a while the sick women were always calm. As a child I was deeply impressed and amazed by this. Then I heard from our country neighbors and from my teachers in town that the whole illness was faked to get out of work, and that it could always be cured by suitable severity. They told various stories to prove it. Later, though, medical specialists told me, to my astonishment, that nothing is faked here. It is a terrible illness that women suffer from, and it is especially widespread among us in Russia. It comes, they said, from the hard lot of peasant women. A woman goes back to exhausting work too soon after a difficult, unnatural childbirth with no help. Add hopeless misery and beatings and the like, which some women could not bear as well as others. The strange, instant cure of the frantic, struggling woman as soon as she was brought to the holy sacrament had been explained to me as malingering and the trickery of the “clericals.” In fact, it probably came about in the most natural way. The women who held her up, and the sick woman herself, were completely certain that the evil spirit inside her could not hold out once she was brought to the sacrament and made to bow down before it. So in a nervous, mentally disturbed woman, the whole body always went into a sort of convulsion, and it was bound to, at the moment of bowing down. The expectation of a miraculous cure and the unquestioning belief that it would come set it off. And it did come, though only for a moment. It was exactly the same now, as soon as the elder touched the sick woman with the stole.
The moment moved many of the women in the crowd to tears of ecstasy. Some reached out to kiss the hem of his robe, and others called out in sing-song voices.
He blessed all of them and talked with a few. He already knew the “possessed” woman. She was from a village just six versts from the monastery, and she had been brought to him before.

“But here is one who has come from far away.” He pointed at a woman who was not at all old but very thin and worn, with a face not just sunburnt but nearly black from the weather. She knelt there staring at the elder without blinking. Her eyes had something almost frenzied in them.

“From far away, Father, from far away! From two hundred miles away. From far away, Father, from far away!” the woman began in a sing-song voice, like someone chanting a dirge. She swayed her head from side to side, her cheek resting on her hand.

Among the peasantry you meet a silent, patient sorrow. It draws into itself and goes still. But there is also a grief that breaks out. From that moment it dissolves in tears and pours itself out in wailing. This is especially common in women. It is not a lighter grief than the silent kind. Lamentations bring comfort only by tearing the heart still more. Such grief does not want consolation. It feeds on its own hopelessness. Lamentations come only from a constant craving to open the wound again.
“You belong to the tradesman class?” asked Father Zossima, looking at her with curiosity.

“We’re townfolk, Father, townfolk. But we’re peasants all the same, even though we live in town. I’ve come to see you, O Father! We heard about you, Father, we heard about you. I’ve buried my little son, and I’ve come on a pilgrimage. I’ve been to three monasteries, and they said to me, ‘Go to them, Nastasya, go to them’—that means to you. So I came. I was at the service yesterday, and today I’ve come to you.”
“What are you weeping for?”

“It’s my little son I’m grieving for, Father. He was three years old—three years all but three months. I’m in anguish for my little boy, Father, for my little boy. He was the last one we had left. We had four, my Nikita and I, and now we have no children. Our dear ones are all gone. I buried the first three without grieving too much, but now that I’ve buried the last one, I can’t forget him. He seems to be standing in front of me all the time. He never leaves me. He’s withered my heart. I look at his little clothes, his little shirt, his little boots, and I wail. I lay out everything that’s left of him, all his little things. I look at them and I wail. I say to Nikita, my husband, ‘Let me go on a pilgrimage, master.’ He’s a driver. We’re not poor, Father, not poor. He drives our own horse. It’s all ours, the horse and the carriage. And what use is it all to us now? My Nikita has started drinking while I’m away. I’m sure of it. It was like that before. The minute I turn my back, he gives in to it. But now I don’t think about him. I left home three months ago. I’ve forgotten him. I’ve forgotten everything. I don’t want to remember. And what would our life together be now? I’m through with him, I’m through. I’m through with all of them. I don’t even want to look at my house and my belongings. I don’t want to see anything at all!”

“Listen, mother,” said the elder. “Once, in olden times, a holy saint saw in the Temple a mother like you. She was weeping for her little one, her only one, whom God had taken. ‘Do you not know,’ said the saint to her, ‘how bold these little ones are before the throne of God? Truly, no one in the Kingdom of Heaven is bolder than they. “You gave us life, O Lord,” they say, “and we had hardly looked at it when You took it back.” And they ask so boldly, and ask again, that God gives them the rank of angels at once. Therefore,’ said the saint, ‘you too, O mother, rejoice and weep no more, for your little son is with the Lord, in the company of the angels.’ That is what the saint said to the weeping mother of old. He was a great saint, and he could not have spoken falsely. So you too, mother, must know that your little one is surely before the throne of God. He is rejoicing, and happy, and praying to God for you. Therefore do not weep, but rejoice.”
The woman listened to him, looking down, her cheek on her hand. She sighed deeply.

“My Nikita tried to comfort me with the very same words as you. ‘You foolish woman,’ he said, ‘why are you crying? Our son is surely singing with the angels before God.’ That’s what he says to me, but he cries himself. I can see he cries just like me. ‘I know, Nikita,’ I said. ‘Where else could he be but with the Lord God? It’s only that here with us he’s not the way he used to sit beside us.’ And if only I could see him one little time, if only I could peep at him one little time, without going up to him, without saying a word, if I could hide in a corner and just see him for one little minute, hear him playing in the yard, calling in his little voice, ‘Mammy, where are you?’ If only I could hear him pattering across the room on his little feet, just once, only once. So often, so often I remember how he used to run to me, shouting and laughing. If only I could hear his little feet, I would know him! But he’s gone, Father, he’s gone, and I’ll never hear him again. Here’s his little sash, but him I’ll never see or hear now.”

She pulled her boy’s little embroidered sash out of her bosom. The moment she looked at it, she began to shake with sobs. She hid her eyes behind her fingers, and the tears came pouring through them in a sudden stream.

“This is Rachel of old,” said the elder, “weeping for her children, and she will not be comforted, because they are not. This is the lot set on earth for you mothers. Do not be comforted. Consolation is not what you need. Weep, and do not be consoled, but weep. Only, each time you weep, be sure to remember that your little son is one of the angels of God. He looks down at you from there and sees you. He rejoices at your tears and points to them for the Lord God to see. For a long while yet you will carry that great mother’s grief. But in the end it will turn into a quiet joy. Your bitter tears will become tears of tender sorrow, which purifies the heart and frees it from sin. And I will pray for the peace of your child’s soul. What was his name?”
“Alexey, Father.”
“A sweet name. Was he named for Alexey, the man of God?”
“Yes, Father.”

“What a saint he was! I will remember him in my prayers, mother, and your grief too, and I will pray for your husband’s health. It is a sin for you to leave him. Your little one will see from heaven that you have abandoned his father, and he will weep over you. Why do you disturb his happiness? He is alive, for the soul lives forever. Though he is not in the house, he is near you, unseen. How can he go into the house when you say you hate it? Where is he to go if he does not find you together, his father and mother? He comes to you in dreams now, and you grieve. But then he will send you gentle dreams. Go to your husband, mother. Go this very day.”

“I will go, Father, as you say. I will go. You’ve gone straight to my heart. My Nikita, my Nikita, you’re waiting for me,” the woman began in her sing-song voice. But the elder had already turned to a very old woman. She was dressed like someone from the town, not like a pilgrim. Her eyes showed that she had come with a purpose and had something to say. She said she was the widow of a non-commissioned officer and lived close by, in town. Her son Vasenka worked in the commissariat and had gone to Irkutsk, in Siberia. He had written twice from there, but now a year had gone by without a word. She had asked about him, but she did not know where the proper place to ask was.

“Just the other day Stepanida Ilyinishna—she’s a rich merchant’s wife—said to me, ‘Go, Prohorovna, and put your son’s name down in the church for prayers, and pray for the peace of his soul as if he were dead. His soul will be troubled,’ she said, ‘and he will write you a letter.’ And Stepanida Ilyinishna told me it was certain, that it had been tried many times. Only I’m in doubt.... Oh, you light of ours! Is it true or false, and would it be right?”

“Do not even think of it. It is shameful to ask such a question. How can anyone pray for the peace of a living soul? And his own mother, too! It is a great sin, close to sorcery. Only because you did not know better are you forgiven. Pray instead to the Queen of Heaven, our swift defense and help, for his good health, and ask her to forgive you for your mistake. And I will tell you something else, Prohorovna. Either your son will soon come back to you, or he will surely send a letter. Go, and from now on be at peace. Your son is alive, I tell you.”
“Dear Father, God reward you, our benefactor, who prays for all of us and for our sins!”

But the elder had already noticed two glowing eyes in the crowd, fixed on him. A young peasant woman, worn out and looking consumptive, was watching him in silence. Her eyes pleaded with him, but she seemed afraid to come closer.
“What is it, my child?”
“Absolve my soul, Father,” she said softly, and slowly sank to her knees and bowed down at his feet. “I have sinned, Father. I am afraid of my sin.”
The elder sat down on the lowest step. The woman crept closer to him, still on her knees.

“I have been a widow for three years,” she began in a half-whisper, with a kind of shudder. “My life with my husband was hard. He was an old man. He used to beat me cruelly. He lay sick, and I thought, looking at him, what if he got well, what if he got up again, what then? And then the thought came to me—”
“Wait!” said the elder, and he put his ear close to her lips.
The woman went on in a low whisper, so low that it was almost impossible to catch anything. She was soon done.
“Three years ago?” asked the elder.
“Three years. At first I didn’t think about it, but now I’ve started to be ill, and the thought never leaves me.”
“Have you come far?”
“Over three hundred miles.”
“Have you told it in confession?”
“I’ve confessed it. Twice I’ve confessed it.”
“Have you been allowed to take Communion?”
“Yes. I’m afraid. I’m afraid to die.”

“Fear nothing, never be afraid, and do not fret. As long as your repentance does not fail, God will forgive everything. There is no sin, and there can be no sin on all the earth, that the Lord will not forgive the truly repentant! No man can commit a sin so great that it uses up the infinite love of God. Can there be a sin that goes beyond the love of God? Think only of repentance, continual repentance, but put fear away completely. Believe that God loves you more than you can imagine, that He loves you with your sin, in your sin. It was said long ago that there is more joy in heaven over one repentant sinner than over ten righteous men. Go, and do not be afraid. Do not be bitter against people. Do not be angry if you are wronged. Forgive the dead man in your heart for whatever wrong he did you. Be truly reconciled with him. If you repent, you love. And if you love, you belong to God. Love atones for everything and saves everything. If I, a sinner like you, am tender with you and pity you, how much more will God. Love is so priceless a treasure that you can buy back the whole world with it, and make amends not only for your own sins but for the sins of others.”
He made the sign of the cross over her three times, took a little ikon from his own neck, and hung it on her. She bowed to the ground without a word.
He rose and looked cheerfully at a healthy peasant woman holding a tiny baby.
“From Vyshegorye, dear Father.”
“Five miles you have dragged yourself, with the baby. What do you want?”

“I came to look at you. I’ve been to see you before—or have you forgotten? You don’t have much of a memory if you’ve forgotten me. They told us you were ill. I thought, I’ll go and see for myself. Now I see you, and you’re not ill! You’ll live another twenty years. God bless you! There are plenty of people praying for you. How could you be ill?”
“I thank you for everything, daughter.”

“By the way, I’ve got something to ask, nothing much. Here are sixty kopecks. Give them, dear Father, to someone poorer than me. I thought on my way here, better to give it through him. He’ll know who to give it to.”
“Thank you, my dear, thank you! You are a good woman. I love you. I will certainly do it. Is that your little girl?”
“My little girl, Father, Lizaveta.”
“May the Lord bless you both, you and your baby Lizaveta! You have made my heart glad, mother. Farewell, dear children, farewell, dear ones.”
He blessed them all and bowed low to them.
